summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis and a history of chronic pain and recurrent nausea, was admitted with nausea, vomiting, and fever attributed to an upper respiratory infection. He reported that febrile illnesses often trigger vomiting, which was unresponsive to ondansetron but improved with promethazine and lorazepam. Initial evaluation revealed no bacterial infection on chest X-ray, urine, or blood work, and he received IV fluids for mild dehydration. Though back pain was not a primary complaint, he experienced a flare in thoracic pain during admission. A detailed discussion about pain management ensued, during which he expressed interest in transitioning from short-acting hydrocodone to a long-acting opioid formulation to stabilize his pain and improve function, though no change was made during the hospitalization. He acknowledged the risks and emphasized his motivation to lose weight and improve his health once pain was better controlled. He engaged in discussions about multidisciplinary strategies, including pain psychology and weight management. He stabilized clinically, remained afebrile, and had no further vomiting. He was discharged home on his prior medications with follow-up planned in primary care and pain psychology.
problems: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
